facts: The famous bronze statue of Robin Hood stands at the base of Nottingham Castle's walls.
The current castle is largely a 17th-century ducal mansion, built after the medieval castle was slighted.
Nottingham's caves, carved into soft sandstone beneath the city, have been used for centuries.
Nottingham has hundreds of man-made caves carved into the sandstone beneath the city.
They have been used over the centuries as tanneries, air raid shelters and pub cellars.
Nottingham station itself is a Grade II listed Edwardian building.
Derby Cathedral has the second-tallest cathedral tower in England after Wells.
Derby has been a centre of Rolls-Royce aero engine manufacturing since the early 20th century.
The city was also home to one of the world's first factories, Lombe's Silk Mill, built in 1721.
Cromford Mill, built by Richard Arkwright in 1771, is considered the world's first successful water-powered cotton spinning factory.
The Derwent Valley Mills are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, seen as the birthplace of the factory system.
Cromford station sits on the scenic line up the Derwent Valley towards Matlock.
Belper's North Mill, built in 1804, is one of the earliest surviving iron-framed buildings in the world.
The town forms part of the Derwent Valley Mills UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Belper was developed by the Strutt family as a model industrial community.

landmark: The Heights of Abraham, Matlock Bath
facts: A cable car climbs from Matlock Bath up to the Heights of Abraham hilltop park and show caverns.
Matlock Bath developed as a spa resort from the 18th century, nicknamed 'the Little Switzerland of England'.
The village sits in a dramatic limestone gorge on the River Derwent.
The spire of St Mary and All Saints Church twists 45 degrees and leans nearly 3 metres off vertical.
Several legends attempt to explain the twist, including one blaming the Devil.
Chesterfield sits at the eastern edge of the Peak District.
Lincoln Cathedral was the tallest building in the world for over 200 years after its central spire was completed.
It holds one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta.
Lincoln's steep, cobbled Steep Hill leads from the station area up to the cathedral quarter.
Lincoln Castle was built by William the Conqueror in 1068, unusually with two mottes.
Visitors can walk the full circuit of its medieval walls.
The castle and cathedral sit together at the top of the city's historic hill.

landmark: Leicester's King Richard III Visitor Centre
facts: King Richard III's remains were discovered beneath a Leicester car park in 2012, later reburied in the cathedral.
The centre tells the story of his life, death at Bosworth, and rediscovery.
Leicester is one of the oldest cities in England, with continuous occupation since Roman times.
The National Space Centre includes the UK's largest planetarium and a 42-metre rocket tower.
Leicester University has a strong tradition in space science research.
Leicester was the first city in the world to be designated an Environment City, in 1990.
St Botolph's Church, nicknamed the 'Boston Stump', has one of the tallest church towers in England.
The Massachusetts city of Boston is named after this Lincolnshire town.
Boston was historically one of England's busiest medieval ports.
Newark Castle withstood three sieges during the English Civil War, remaining loyal to the King throughout.
King John died at the castle in 1216.
Newark Castle station sits right beside the castle ruins on the River Trent.
Stamford is widely regarded as one of the finest Georgian stone towns in England.
It was used as a filming location for the BBC's Middlemarch and Pride and Prejudice adaptations.
The nearby Burghley House is one of England's grandest Elizabethan houses.
Burghley House was built for William Cecil, chief advisor to Elizabeth I, completed in 1587.
It hosts the Burghley Horse Trials, one of the world's leading equestrian events, each September.
The house holds one of the largest private art collections in Europe.

landmark: Melton Mowbray pork pies & Stilton cheese
facts: Melton Mowbray pork pies have Protected Geographical Indication status, like Champagne or Parma ham.
The town is also recognised as the historic home of Stilton cheese production.
Melton Mowbray calls itself the 'Rural Capital of Food' in England.
Grimsby was once the largest fishing port in the world during the early 20th century.
The heritage centre recreates conditions aboard a real 1950s trawler.
Grimsby's dock tower, built in 1852, remains a landmark visible across the town.
Skegness's 'Jolly Fisherman' poster, from 1908, remains one of Britain's most famous seaside advertising images.
The town's beach stretches for several miles along the Lincolnshire coast.
Skegness is the eastern terminus of a branch line from Nottingham via Grantham.
Burton-on-Trent's water uniquely suits pale ale brewing, helping it become England's brewing capital in the 19th century.
The town was once home to dozens of breweries, several of which remain today.
The National Brewery Centre tells the story of Burton's beer-making history.
Loughborough is home to the Great Central Railway, one of the few heritage lines in Britain to run genuine double-track mainline services.
The town's bellfoundry, still working today, has cast bells for buildings worldwide, including St Paul's Cathedral.
Loughborough University is renowned internationally for its sports science programmes.
Oakham Castle's Great Hall displays an unusual collection of ceremonial horseshoes, a centuries-old local tradition.
By ancient custom, any peer visiting Oakham for the first time must forfeit a horseshoe.
Oakham is the county town of Rutland, England's smallest historic county.
Kettering was historically a major centre of the boot and shoe manufacturing industry.
The town's Alfred East Art Gallery is named after the local landscape painter.
Kettering is a key stop on the Midland Main Line between London and Sheffield.
Market Harborough's timber-framed Old Grammar School, built in 1614, stands on stilts above the market place.
The town developed at a key crossroads in medieval times.
Market Harborough sits close to the Leicestershire and Northamptonshire border.
Corby's steelworks drew large numbers of Scottish workers in the 1930s, giving the town a distinctive Scottish accent influence.
The town's population grew rapidly during its industrial boom in the mid-20th century.
Corby's railway station reopened in 2009 after decades without a regular passenger service.
Wellingborough sits in the Nene Valley, historically known for shoe manufacturing alongside nearby Kettering.
The town's All Hallows Church has origins dating back over 800 years.
Wellingborough is a stop on the Midland Main Line.
Uttoxeter Racecourse specialises in National Hunt (jump) racing.
The town's market charter dates back to the 12th century.
Uttoxeter sits on the River Dove in Staffordshire.
Alton Towers, one of the UK's largest theme parks, grew from the grounds of a 19th-century Gothic mansion.
The gardens were laid out by the Earls of Shrewsbury from the 1810s onward.
Uttoxeter is the nearest railway station, with the park reached by road.
Poet Lord Byron is buried at St Mary Magdalene Church in Hucknall, near the family seat at Newstead Abbey.
Hucknall developed rapidly as a coal mining town in the 19th and 20th centuries.
The town sits just north of Nottingham.
Newstead Abbey was the ancestral home of the poet Lord Byron, inherited in 1798.
The house was converted from a medieval Augustinian priory after the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
Its grounds include ornamental lakes and gardens open to the public.
Mansfield sits close to Sherwood Forest, associated with the legend of Robin Hood.
The town was historically a centre of textile and framework knitting industries.
Mansfield's railway station reopened in 1995 after decades of closure, on the reinstated Robin Hood Line.
Ilkeston has held a market charter since 1252.
The town was historically linked to lace-making and coal mining in the Erewash Valley.
Ilkeston station reopened in 2017 after over 50 years without passenger services.
Long Eaton grew rapidly around lace manufacturing in the 19th century.
The town sits on the River Erewash, close to the Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire border.
Long Eaton is also known for its furniture and upholstery trade.
Attenborough Nature Reserve was created from former gravel pits along the River Trent.
It is named after the village, not naturalist Sir David Attenborough, though he has visited and supported it.
The reserve is an important site for wetland birds close to Nottingham.
Beeston is home to a major campus of the University of Nottingham.
The town developed around lace and pharmaceutical manufacturing, including the founders of Boots.
Beeston sits just west of Nottingham city centre.
John Taylor & Co in Loughborough is one of the oldest working bellfoundries in the world.
It cast the Great Paul bell for St Paul's Cathedral, once the largest bell in Britain.
The foundry has operated on its current site since 1859.
Spalding was once the centre of England's bulb-growing industry, especially tulips.
The town historically held a major Flower Parade each spring.
Spalding sits in the flat, fertile Lincolnshire Fens.
St Denys' Church in Sleaford has one of the earliest surviving examples of window tracery in England.
Sleaford sits at the heart of Lincolnshire's agricultural land.
The town was historically an important market centre for the surrounding Fens.
Bulwell has a medieval market cross still standing in its town centre.
The suburb developed around coal mining and framework knitting industries.
Bulwell sits on the northern edge of Nottingham.
Alfreton was historically a centre of coal mining in the Derbyshire coalfield.
The town sits close to the Nottinghamshire border in the Amber Valley.
Alfreton railway station serves the wider Amber Valley district.
Ambergate was historically an important railway junction where lines to Manchester and Derby diverged.
The village sits at the confluence of the Rivers Derwent and Amber.
Ambergate lies within the Derwent Valley Mills UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Duffield retains a well-preserved Georgian village centre.
The remains of Duffield Castle, once one of the largest Norman keeps in England, lie nearby.
Duffield sits on the River Derwent, north of Derby.
Willington was historically home to large coal-fired power stations on the River Trent, since demolished.
The village sits close to Repton, home to one of England's oldest public schools.
Willington station serves the South Derbyshire countryside.
Mary, Queen of Scots was imprisoned at Tutbury Castle on several occasions in the 1560s and 1580s.
The castle overlooks the Dove Valley on the Staffordshire and Derbyshire border.
Tutbury is also known for its glass-making tradition.
Barrow-upon-Soar was once a centre of lime burning and quarrying along the River Soar.
Ichthyosaur fossils have been found in the village's former quarries.
Barrow-upon-Soar sits between Leicester and Loughborough.
Syston sits close to where the Grand Union Canal's Leicester line meets the River Soar Navigation.
The town grew as a residential suburb of Leicester in the 19th and 20th centuries.
Syston is on the Midland Main Line just north of Leicester.
East Midlands Parkway station opened in 2009 to serve East Midlands Airport and the surrounding area.
The station sits close to the cooling towers of Ratcliffe-on-Soar Power Station.
It provides a park-and-ride style interchange between road and rail.
The Grimsby Dock Tower, completed in 1852, was modelled on the Palazzo Pubblico tower in Siena.
It originally supplied hydraulic power to operate the dock's lock gates.
Grimsby's fishing fleet was once the largest in the world.
Barton-on-Humber sits on the south bank of the Humber, opposite Hull, close to the Humber Bridge.
St Peter's Church in the town has an Anglo-Saxon tower among the oldest standing structures of its kind in England.
Barton was a significant medieval port before trade shifted to Hull and Grimsby.
Bottesford's church holds elaborate tombs of the Earls of Rutland from nearby Belvoir Castle.
The village sits in the fertile Vale of Belvoir, known for its agriculture.
Bottesford has the tallest parish church spire in Leicestershire.
Kelham Island Museum tells the story of Sheffield's steel and industrial heritage on an artificial island in the River Don.
It houses the River Don Engine, once the most powerful working steam engine in Europe.
Sheffield is famous worldwide for pioneering stainless steel, invented there in 1913.
